source.version: Journal version of record: PNAS Nexus, 2025, Vol. 4, No. 10, pgaf316, Research Report, advance access publication 28 October 2025 (received March 28, 2025; accepted September 11, 2025). The paper says an earlier version was posted at https://ssrn.com/abstract=5104064 (p. 10, Preprints).
source.title_on_document: Experimental evidence of the effects of large language models versus web search on depth of learning

supplement.where: "Supplementary material is available at PNAS Nexus online." (p. 10, Supplementary Material). Data, surveys, and preregistrations on OSF (p. 10, Data Availability; no URL printed).
supplement.holds: Three preregistered replications reported only there (replication of experiment 1 on healthier lifestyle with a third LLM-plus-real-time-web-links arm, n = 2,402; replication of experiment 1 on financial scams, n = 1,976; conceptual replication of experiment 4, n = 1,258), full survey instruments and stimuli, the experiment 2 mediation model, and the ex post analysis controlling for number of websites visited. The main text reports arm means, F statistics, and P values but no standard deviations or standard errors for any outcome; any SDs would have to come from the supplement or OSF data.

paper_design_summary: Online (Prolific) and lab participants were randomly assigned to learn how to plant a vegetable garden or lead a healthier lifestyle either from an LLM (ChatGPT, a simulated GPT-4o summary, or Google AI Overview) or from web links (real or simulated Google search), and then wrote advice for a friend on a separate page. The advice texts were scored with computed measures: within-condition pairwise cosine similarity of LDA topic vectors, pairwise Levenshtein edit distance, word count, and named-entity counts. In experiment 4, a separate MTurk sample rated advice texts from experiment 3 for helpfulness, informativeness, trust, and willingness to adopt.

studies.label: Experiment 1 (real ChatGPT vs real Google search, vegetable garden advice, Prolific)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Search tool used to learn about the topic before writing advice: in-house ChatGPT interface vs actual Google search results
assignment.quote: Participants were 1,136 members of the Prolific panel who were randomly assigned to learn about a topic using either ChatGPT or Google and then to write advice for their friend on it

arms.name: ChatGPT
arms.description: Interactive ChatGPT interface programmed into the Qualtrics survey (OpenAI Chat Completion API, GPT-3.5-turbo); as many prompts as wished; then wrote advice

arms.name: Google
arms.description: Actual Google search results via an in-house site (Google Custom Search JSON API), 10 links per page; browse freely and re-query; then wrote advice

participants.exclusions: 32 participants excluded for failing attention checks, per the preregistered criteria (1,136 to 1,104). Arm sizes are not printed. The paper reports Mage = 42.40 and 46% female for the 1,136 and Mage = 42.40 and 53% female for the 1,104.
participants.quote: we excluded 32 participants for failing attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 1,104 participants

ai_tool.name_model: In-house ChatGPT interface using OpenAI's Chat Completion API with GPT-3.5-turbo (note c, p. 9)
ai_tool.how_used: Used as a search tool to learn about the topic before writing; participants could submit as many prompts as they wished (mean 2.06 prompts). Advice was written afterward on a separate step of the survey.

task.description: Imagine a friend seeks advice on how to plant a vegetable garden; search for information, then write advice for the friend (free text).
task.duration: Not fixed. Mean search time 742.81 s (Google) vs 585.41 s (ChatGPT); mean advice-writing time 246.81 s vs 221.40 s (pp. 4-5).

outcomes.name: Topical similarity of advice across writers (average pairwise cosine similarity of LDA topic vectors within condition)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modeling run separately for each condition, topic distributions reduced by PCA to the same number of topics, then average pairwise cosine similarity between all pairs of advice within each condition. Lower = more unique. The vectors are LDA topic vectors, not neural embeddings.
outcomes.delay: Same session, advice written right after the search task

contrasts.reported: cosine similarity: M Google = 0.057, M GPT = 0.159; F(1, 1,102) = 168.46, P < 0.001

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise cosine similarity of PCA-reduced LDA topic vectors (higher = more similar = less diverse)
diversity_detail.embedding_model: LDA topic model fitted separately per condition, reduced with PCA
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of advice within each condition
diversity_detail.uncertainty: One-way F test with df (1, 1,102), i.e. one score per advice text; the paper does not describe how per-text scores were formed
diversity_detail.notes: Direction coded on diversity: the LLM arm has higher similarity, so lower diversity. Description of the measure is on p. 4.

outcomes.name: Semantic uniqueness of advice across writers (average pairwise Levenshtein edit distance within condition)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average pairwise Levenshtein edit distance between all pairs of advice within each condition; higher = greater dissimilarity in the words used. The paper calls it a convergent measure of originality.

contrasts.reported: Levenshtein edit distance: M Google = 531.86, M GPT = 481.59; F(1, 1,102) = 13.67, P < 0.001

diversity_detail.metric: Average pairwise Levenshtein edit distance (higher = more dissimilar = more diverse)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of advice within each condition
diversity_detail.uncertainty: One-way F test with df (1, 1,102); per-text score construction not described
diversity_detail.notes: LLM arm has lower edit distance, so lower diversity. Description on p. 4.

outcomes.name: Word count of advice
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of words computed with LIWC 2022 (a computed text count, not a creativity scoring model); the paper cites Dumas et al. (2021) on measuring elaboration.

outcomes.name: References to facts in advice (unique named entities)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: spaCy pretrained Named Entity Recognition: count of words or word pairs in seven predefined categories plus a topic-specific gardening domain (note d). The paper treats it as a marker of depth of knowledge, not creativity.

contrasts.reported: unique entities: M Google = 0.718, M GPT = 0.464; F(1, 1,102) = 6.66, P = 0.010

eligibility.reason: Experiments 1-3 randomly assign individuals to learn from an LLM (ChatGPT, a GPT-4o summary, or Google AI Overview) versus web links before writing advice (pp. 3, 6, 7), with 1,104, 1,979, and 250 people analyzed. The advice texts are compared across writers for similarity with computed measures (LDA-topic cosine similarity, Levenshtein distance), which fits the codebook's rule that writing tasks compared across writers for similarity belong. The AI was used in a learning phase before writing, so the outcomes are after_ai and the comparison is ai_vs_active (web search). Judgment calls for the reviewer: whether advice writing counts as a creative task, and whether AI use as a search tool counts as AI assistance on the task.

one_line_finding: Advice written after learning from an LLM rather than web links was more similar across writers (pairwise topical cosine similarity 0.159 vs 0.057 in experiment 1, p. 5; 0.224 vs 0.072 in experiment 2, p. 6; 0.214 vs 0.073 in experiment 3, p. 7), had lower pairwise Levenshtein distance, and was shorter.
open_questions: AI availability during writing: the paper describes writing as a step after the search task (S1: 'Once participants finished the search task, they proceeded to write their advice', p. 3; S2: 'proceed to a separate page', p. 6; S3: 'return to the survey tab', p. 7) but never states that the search tool was inaccessible while writing. In S3 the Google tab was a separate browser tab. I coded ai_available_when_produced = 'no' and question = after_ai.

Is advice on planting a vegetable garden or leading a healthier lifestyle a creative task? The paper frames the outcome as depth of learning and 'originality' of advice; the codebook admits writing tasks compared across writers for similarity.

The diversity measure fits LDA separately per condition and reduces each condition's topic vectors with PCA before computing within-condition cosine similarity (p. 4), so the two arms' vectors are not in a common topic space. The F tests have df (1, N-2), implying one score per text, but the paper does not say how per-text scores were formed.

Experiment 2: the control arm's six web articles were GPT-4o rewrites of the same 291-word GPT-4o summary (p. 6), so both arms read AI-generated content; only the format differs. Comparison coded ai_vs_active with the control as other_aid.
S3 population: 'behavioral lab panel at an east-coast university' (Mage 22.75); the paper does not say they are students. Coded general_public.
S5 and S6 design class (online_rct) is inferred from 'replications of experiment 1'; the main text does not state the platform, and S6's randomization is not stated in the main text.
notes: Inconsistencies in the PDF: total n is 10,462 in the abstract (p. 1) but 10,426 in the introduction (p. 2). The analyzed counts of S1-S4 (1,104 + 1,979 + 250 + 1,493) plus the supplementary ns (2,402 + 1,976 + 1,258) sum to 10,462, which suggests the supplementary ns are analyzed counts, but the PDF does not say so, so I left them null. In S1 the paper reports 46% female for the 1,136 and 53% female for the 1,104 with the same mean age (p. 3). In the experiment 4 chi-square result the labels look reversed: 'the observed proportion of LLM-based advice [50.6%, n = 756 ...] being significantly lower than that of advice based on web links [24.6%, n = 367 ...]' (p. 8); recorded verbatim. Experiment 4 rates the advice of experiment 3 participants, so S4 shares the writer sample of S3 within this paper; no participants are shared with other papers. Experiment 1 uses GPT-3.5-turbo (note c, p. 9) although the limitations paragraph mentions 'actual LLMs (e.g. GPT-4o)' (p. 9). Self-reported outcomes (felt learning, ownership, effort, comprehensiveness) and time-on-task are not scored on the output and are not listed. No SDs or SEs are printed in the main text for any outcome; only arm means, F statistics, and P values. Arm sizes are printed only for experiment 3 (125 texts each, p. 8). The paper names no primary outcome among the text measures; it calls self-reported depth of learning 'the focal construct of interest' (p. 3). The supplementary studies (S5-S7) have no outcome statistics in this PDF, so their outcome lists are empty.
